pages.x: For centuries the Shang kings ruled the plain of the Yellow River. At their last capital, near today's Anyang, they wrote questions to their ancestors on turtle shells and ox bones, the oldest Chinese writing we have, and honoured them with offerings of bronze, wine and human sacrifice.

In the Wei valley to the west, the Zhou grew strong under King Wen. His son, King Wu, gathered allies against the last Shang king, Di Xin, at the ford of Mengjin on the Yellow River, and in about 1046 BC led them east.

Later writers said that Di Xin dug a lake of wine and hung meat from the trees, so that his guests could feast as they chased each other naked, and that he roasted his critics on a burning bronze pillar. The tales were told by the winners, and may be mostly legend.

King Wu's army met the Shang host at Muye, south of the Shang capital. The Shang army was far larger, but many of its soldiers, it is said, turned their spears around and joined the Zhou. Di Xin fled to his palace, put on his robes of jade, and burned himself to death.

To explain their right to rule, the Zhou taught that Heaven gives its mandate to a just ruler, and takes it away from a wicked one. The idea lasted three thousand years: every new dynasty in China claimed the Mandate, and floods, famines and revolts were read as signs that it had been lost.

King Wu died a few years later, leaving a boy king. His brother, the Duke of Zhou, ruled for him, crushed a revolt by Shang loyalists and his own brothers, and then, it is said, handed power back when the king came of age. Confucius later held him up as the perfect minister.

The Zhou dynasty lasted almost 800 years, longer than any other in Chinese history. The idea it gave China, that a ruler's right to rule depends on ruling well, became the backbone of Chinese political thought, and the Shang were remembered as a warning.

It gave China the Mandate of Heaven
